name: Aerial dance

narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

instructor.rule: counts out loud; demonstrates front and back; three slow repetitions before tempo; one correction at a time

scenes.title: Cold open
narration: Defying gravity through the art of aerial dance.
This is aerial dance, spanning from the 1970s to the present.
on_screen: Hero video — MISSING
Title card: Aerial dance · United States · 1970s–present

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Aerial dance began in the United States during the 1970s.
Trisha Brown's equipment pieces from 1968 to 1971 are early examples of using suspension to explore everyday movement.
Terry Sendgraff invented the motivity trapeze in the early 1970s, enabling new forms of aerial rotation and flight.
on_screen: Map: United States · Global
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Performances take place in festivals, contemporary dance theaters, and public architectural spaces.
Dancers use this form to communicate contemporary ideas, explore the body's relationship with the environment, and challenge traditional dance boundaries.
It remains a living tradition today.
on_screen: Footage: File:VideoCervantino 1.webm (https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/b9/VideoCervantino_1.webm?utm_source=commons.wikimedia.org&utm_campaign=imageinfo&utm_content=original)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers use apparatuses such as harnesses, silks, or trapezes.
Movements include ascensions, inversions, and controlled drops.
The dancer must manage their center of gravity in response to the apparatus's motion.
Watch for French climb, Star drop.
on_screen: Hero video — MISSING
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Three-dimensional; uses vertical and horizontal paths.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key figures include pioneer Trisha Brown, motivity trapeze inventor Terry Sendgraff, vertical dance network founder Wanda Moretti, Joanna Haigood of Zaccho Dance Theatre, Amelia Rudolph of Project Bandaloop, and Sally Jacques of Blue Lapis Light.
The discipline is practiced globally, with major hubs in the United States, Italy, France, and the United Kingdom.
Aerial dance descends from modern dance, with influences from circus arts, rock climbing, and gymnastics.

scenes.title: Welcome
narration: Chapter 1 covers first steps, focusing on foundational grip and core strength.

scenes.title: Body and posture
narration: Suspension requires an engaged core and precise alignment.
Grip strength and arm endurance are essential.
These elements are central to balance and initiating movement in the air.

scenes.title: Step B — the next layer

music_brief.purpose: copyright-free soundtrack with the same DNA as the tradition's music — an original creation, not a reproduction
music_brief.prompt: Original instrumental composition in the musical world of Aerial dance (United States). Mood: contemporary, experimental. New melody, new arrangement: do not quote or imitate any specific recorded song; keep the idiom, the instruments, the pulse and the proportions.

tracks.use: chapters: dance it to the music

rules: Original composition only — no sampling, no melody of any existing recording, no lyrics from any song.
Traditional public-domain tunes may be used only when the profile names them and a public-domain source is on file; otherwise compose new material in the idiom.
Keep the proportions true: the meter, the tempo range and the instrument roles the sources describe.
Label every generated track with the tool, the date and this brief, so provenance is always clear.
